paragraphs.first_sentence: We first characterized the SPY series and the HMM-WJ calibrated to its training window (Fig.~\ref{fig:empirical_motivation}; Table~\ref{tab:descriptive_stats})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The duration $\lambda$ was likewise a fitted parameter of the objective, not an estimate of how long observed high-volatility periods last.

paragraphs.first_sentence: We compared the calibrated HMM-WJ with seven alternative generators on the training window, using $1{,}000$ paths of $2{,}766$ trading days (Table~\ref{tab:model_comparison}; Fig.~\ref{fig:model_comparison})
paragraphs.last_sentence: Both HMM variants also reproduced the observed skewness of $-0.75$ without a skewness parameter, because the state means and scales estimated from the asymmetric series carried its asymmetry into the mixture (Online Appendix~\ref{sec:supp-generator}; Table~\ref{tab:supp-generator-quantities}).

paragraphs.first_sentence: Jump episodes traded a small loss of marginal fit for better temporal fit in training (Table~\ref{tab:model_comparison}; Fig.~\ref{fig:model_comparison}b)
paragraphs.last_sentence: At the realized share of about one quarter, the mean path kurtosis of $7.5$ lay slightly below the observed $7.7$ (Table~\ref{tab:model_comparison}).

paragraphs.first_sentence: To test whether the HMM results depended on the state partition, we refitted both HMM variants for $N$ from $30$ to $200$ states (Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity_n})
paragraphs.last_sentence: It therefore did not establish a state count for the other assets, which also used $N=100$, or for shorter histories, which would leave fewer observations per state.

paragraphs.first_sentence: To test whether the distributional fit held on data not used for fitting, we compared $249$-day paths from the frozen models with the $249$ held-out SPY returns from $2025$ (Table~\ref{tab:model_comparison}; Fig.~\ref{fig:statistical_validation})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The six-method composition comparison used the no-jump variant to keep per-ticker jump calibration out of the comparison, and a separate multi-asset comparison evaluated the transfer of jump settings.

paragraphs.first_sentence: We compared six composition methods on the $423$ non-market assets of the training universe to test whether hybrid composition preserved generator variance while recovering the calibrated market loading (Table~\ref{tab:aggregate}; Fig.~\ref{fig:preservation})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The correlation between generator draws and the observed market path averaged near zero for every asset (Fig.~\ref{fig:cov_diag}), which supported the zero-covariance assumption on average but not on each path.

paragraphs.first_sentence: The methods differed more in distributional fit than in factor recovery (Table~\ref{tab:aggregate}; Fig.~\ref{fig:tails})
paragraphs.last_sentence: Its median $R^2$ error fell between those of the naive and Gaussian methods, because the variance-preserving branch targets the generator variance rather than the observed $R^2$.

paragraphs.first_sentence: Fitting the OLS residuals directly needs no correction, because those residuals already exclude the market component, and two of the three residual-fit methods were competitive with hybrid composition (Tables~\ref{tab:aggregate} and~\ref{tab:centering_control})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The correction therefore improved on naive composition without a second generator fit, but hybrid composition trailed JumpHMM-on-residuals under both mean treatments and also trailed block bootstrap after centering.

paragraphs.first_sentence: The emission fallback rules were triggered only in full-return generators, so they could have handicapped naive and hybrid composition relative to the residual-fit methods (Tables~\ref{tab:fallback_assets} and~\ref{tab:fallback_sensitivity})
paragraphs.last_sentence: Both the main comparison and this check used training histories only; the holdout evaluation tested whether the advantage of hybrid over naive composition persisted beyond the fitting period.

paragraphs.first_sentence: To test out-of-sample generalization without refitting or look-ahead bias, we froze the fitted models and SIM parameters before evaluating them against $416$ complete asset histories from $2025$ (Table~\ref{tab:oos_composition})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The rise from training blocks to $2025$ therefore did not hold for every asset.

paragraphs.first_sentence: To test whether the holdout improvement over naive composition extended to reliable tail thresholds, we estimated per-ticker one-day left-tail Value-at-Risk (VaR) thresholds from $5{,}000$ separate $249$-day paths and counted exceedances on the observed $2025$ histories (Table~\ref{tab:var})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The cross-asset standard deviations of the exceedance rates described how realized rates varied among assets; they did not test miscalibration or validate coverage in other periods.

paragraphs.last_sentence: The holdout therefore judged the transferred settings on few episode paths and a single year of observed data, and it could not establish their behavior in other market periods.

paragraphs.first_sentence: We examined how the branch-selection threshold $R^2_{\mathrm{preserve}}$ assigned assets to branches in the observed universe and whether any value of the variance floor $f$ triggered clipping (Figs.~\ref{fig:r2_distribution} and~\ref{fig:branch_map}; Table~\ref{tab:branch})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The empirical evaluation of the $R^2$-preserving branch was therefore limited to two assets, and the observed market variance never activated clipping.

paragraphs.first_sentence: Because only two real assets used the $R^2$-preserving branch, we also checked it on a synthetic grid with known loading and $R^2$ (Table~\ref{tab:tracker_grid})
paragraphs.last_sentence: The grid therefore checked the implementation and finite-sample accuracy of the $R^2$-preserving formula under a restricted Gaussian construction; it did not exercise full-return HMM fitting, non-unit residual scaling, or simulated market paths.
